results.title: We asked ~50 GPU providers for B300 pricing. Here's the map | TheAI Blog
highlights:
## The visible market: public on-demand

Only a handful of providers publish an on-demand B300 price at all. As of the snapshot:

| Provider | On-demand, $/GPU·hr |
| --- | --- |
| Hyperstack | $7.40 |
| Verda | $7.50 |
| Nebius | $7.85 |
| AWS (Capacity Blocks) | $14.04 |

Independent price trackers put the market median around $7.85/GPU·hr — up roughly 57% since November. The floor across trackers has hovered in the $6.94–7.39 range for months. That's the market you can see with a browser.

It is worth pausing on the AWS number: a Capacity Block at $14.04 is roughly double the neocloud rate for the same silicon. That premium buys ecosystem integration, not faster matrix multiplies.

## The invisible market: where the cheap B300s live

Everyone has heard that B300s trade "below $5". It's true — and almost none of it is rental.

Every quote we received under $5.50/GPU·hr came with the same structure: a 2-to-5-year commitment and a 20–40% down payment, wired up front. At that point you're not renting a GPU; you're taking out a mortgage on one, with the residual-value risk quietly transferred to you. Given how fast this hardware generation cycle runs — look up what an H100 rents for today versus its 2023 sticker — a five-year lock on any accelerator is a serious bet: make it with your eyes open.

And the middle of the term curve is nearly empty. Twelve-month wholesale offers — the term most teams actually want — were almost extinct in our scan: single digits of offers across ~50 providers. The market has bifurcated into "right now, at a premium" and "half a decade, at a discount," with very little honest ground between.

...

The subtlest finding, and the one price tables never show: a published on-demand price is not the same thing as an available GPU.

A meaningful share of "on-demand B300" listings today lead to a queue, a "request access" form, or quiet regional stockouts. The price is real; the GPU isn't. You can be looking at a $7+ rate and be unable to deploy at any price — expensive and out of stock at the same time. When you evaluate a provider, the question isn't "what's the number on the page" but "what happens when I click launch."

...

Our takeaway from fifty conversations: the market offers "expensive," "3-year lock-in," and "out of stock" — frequently all at once. The

...

For genuinely available on-demand capacity: public rates cluster at $6.94–7.85/GPU·hr. Reserved rates depend on the term and the prepayment; our current ones are on the rate card.

results.title: The same GPU costs up to 2× more depending on where you rent it | Price of Compute
highlights:
On the day we wrote this, an H100 PCIe rented for $2.00/hr on one tracked provider and $3.29/hr on another — a 1.6× spread on identical silicon. The A100 80GB SXM spread 1.8× ($1.59 to $2.79). These aren’t stale listings; they’re simultaneous, bookable list prices, and some version of this spread appears in our provider matrix every single day.

Why doesn’t it arbitrage away? Because a GPU-hour isn’t actually a commodity — yet. The spread decomposes into real differences: reliability tiers (a marketplace host and an enterprise SLA are different products), interconnect and cluster context (the same card in an InfiniBand pod is worth more than in a lone box), switching costs (data gravity, image rebuilds, quota relationships), and plain information friction — most renters simply don’t see today’s table.

The interesting question is which part of the spread is real quality difference and which part is friction that transparency erodes. Our read of the record so far: the floor moves first on marketplaces, then list-price providers follow in discrete cuts (the events feed catches each one). The spread compresses slowly — but it compresses.

Practically: if your workload tolerates interruption, the spread is free money (spot runs ~40–50% under on-demand on top of choosing the cheap provider — the calculator multiplies it out for your run). If it doesn’t, you’re paying for the tier, not overpaying for the GPU — and now you know exactly how much.

results.title: The GPU Price Crash of 2025 and Why It Reversed - AIVory
highlights:
## The crash: 2023 to late 2025

In early 2023, an H100 rented for roughly $8/hr. Every company with a machine learning team had placed massive GPU orders simultaneously. Nvidia could not ship fast enough. Prices were absurd.

Then the supply caught up. All those orders arrived. Cloud providers, GPU brokers, and sovereign AI clusters all came online within the same 12-month window. The market went from scarcity to glut almost overnight.

By late 2025, one-year contract rates for H100s had fallen to $1.70/hr - a 75-80% crash from peak. Spot prices on marketplaces like Vast.ai dipped below $1.85/hr. Lambda Labs was listing on-demand H100s at $2.99-$3.99/hr while AWS still charged $6.88/hr for the same card.

The oversupply was real. Brokers who had pre-purchased thousands of GPUs were renting them at a loss just to cover power bills.

## H100 pricing across providers (mid-2025 to mid-2026)

| Provider | Type | Mid-2025 ($/hr) | Mid-2026 ($/hr) | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS (p5.48xlarge) | On-demand | $6.88 | $6.98 | +1.5% |
| Lambda Labs | On-demand | $2.99 | $3.99 | +33% |
| CoreWeave | 1-year contract | $1.70 | ~$2.40 | +41% |
| Vast.ai | Spot | $1.85 | $2.50-3.20 | +35-73% |
| Nvidia DGX Cloud | On-demand | ~$3.70 | ~$4.40 | +19% |

Spot pricing saves 50-70% over on-demand across all providers. That spread has held steady through both the crash and the reversal. I covered the mechanics of that spread in Spot GPU Pricing Explained.

## The reversal: 2026

Three things happened at once.

Nvidia raised the floor. In early 2026, Nvidia announced roughly a 20% price increase on H100 rental rates through its DGX Cloud and partner programs. That reset the baseline for everyone downstream.

Blackwell demand ate the surplus. New model architectures - reasoning models, multi-modal systems, long-context inference - need more compute per query. The University of Rhode Island measured GPT-5 class queries at 18.35 Wh average versus 2.12 Wh for GPT-4. That is 8.6x more energy per query, which translates directly to more GPU-hours consumed per dollar of API revenue.

Training runs got bigger again. Frontier labs resumed large pre-training runs on Blackwell clusters. That pulled supply out of the rental market. Blackwell spot rates jumped 48% in 60 days - from $2.75/hr to $4.08/hr.

One-year H100 contracts climbed roughly 40% off their late-2025 lows. The crash was over.

...

The 2023-2025 crash was a supply overshoot. The 2026 reversal is demand catching up. Neither was permanent.

Blackwell supply will ramp through late 2026 and into 2027. When it does, expect another pricing correction downward - probably not as steep as the H100 crash, because Nvidia learned from the oversupply cycle and is managing allocation more tightly.

The pattern is clear: GPU pricing follows semiconductor cycles, not software pricing logic. Plan for 18-month swings of 30-50% in either direction. Lock in contracts when prices are low. Use spot when they are high. And do not assume today’s price is tomorrow’s price.

results.title: AI: The ‘Dwarkesh’ Compute Demand Bull Case (part 2). AI-RTZ #1174
highlights:
Dwarkesh Patel argued this week that compute might get 10x more expensive, and the piece has drawn prominent industry reactions and close examinations for a reason. His math is as follows:

Frontier lab revenue is compounding at roughly 10x a year (particularly frontier AI lab Anthropic for now). Compute supply grows about 3x a year, decomposed as roughly 1.4x from Moore’s Law, 1.2x from new fabs, and 1.8x from wafer reallocation toward AI. If revenue compounds at 10x while capacity compounds at 3x, something has to c lear the gap, and price is the obvious release valve. 

His pointiest version of the claim: compute that can do human-level software engineering should command something like human-level economics. On that logic an H100 could justify around 250 thousand dollars a year in rent, roughly 15x today’s spot price.

And he points to evidence already on the tape: GPU spot prices up 40 percent plus since February. Google reportedly paying about twice spot on its SpaceX rentals. Anthropic’s inference margins going from about 40 percent to above 80 in a year. Buyers locking multi-year capacity now, which is what you do when you expect prices to rise. Plus the wall behind it all: AI taking about 86 percent of advanced node wafer capacity by late 2027.

...

1. Look at who pays these prices, and why. As I wrote yesterday, today’s premiums are desperation prices, paid by OpenAI and Anthropic in their mega-AI IPO windows, especially compute-throttled Anthropic. Windows close. Post-IPO, the same buyers get price-disciplined.
2. Price umbrellas invite supply. As I have written, 30 to 50 million dollars per megawatt-year summons every builder with a balance sheet. Elon is first, not last.
3. Per-token deflation never stops. Every model generation and silicon generation cuts the cost of producing a token. ‘Renting an H100’ is the wrong unit of account over any multi-year horizon, and Dwarkesh’s own examiners make the same distinction: token prices can fall while frontier compute stays tight. Both things happen.
4. Customer silicon compounds. TPUs, Trainium, Maia, and now Anthropic’s own chips. The ‘Frenemies’ build their own exits from spot pricing, every year.
5. The revealed preference. Google and Anthropic rent Elon’s racks on 90-day cancellation clauses. Nobody betting on decade-long scarcity signs a 90-day out.
6. History and China. Dwarkesh concedes it himself: bets on permanent scarcity usually lose to ingenuity, the Simon-Ehrlich lesson. And the Chinese open-weight models keep pressing from below. Yes, DeepSeek just raised prices, which helps his case short-term. But the larger frame, as I argued in the Race to Zero piece, is a WIDENING pricing spectrum, not a curve that moves 10x in either direction. 
7. The labor peg is wobbly. The 250 thousand dollar H100 assumes AI labor prices at human labor rates. Competition among a dozen labs selling the same capability is precisely what breaks that peg. Monopoly rents require a monopoly.
8. This is not all ‘Mainframe AI’. Dwarkesh’s math treats essentially all inference as data center load. But as I have argued since the earliest days of this newsletter, this wave adds a ‘Local AI’ compute stage alongside the ‘Mainframe AI’ stage, and unlike the mainframe-to-PC-to-smartphone transitions that took decades, this one is being measured in years. Nvidia and Microsoft are already building the local AI computers. Yes, ‘RAMageddon’ and the memory shortages temper the pace, as I wrote this past week about Rubin Ultra. But the direction is real, and every inference workload that moves onto a device EXITS the data center pricing equation entirely.
9. The winner-take-all assumption. The bull case quietly assumes the frontier models take most of the world’s compute load at their desired prices, because customers ‘go with the best’ for everything. That is exactly what Microsoft is now arguing against, picking a side against the frontier labs, and what Palantir and the enterprise camp have been shouting, as I covered in the ‘Us vs Them’ pieces. Enterprises in law, medicine, finance and every domain beyond tech are waking up to the pattern: hand the frontier labs your data and your business IP, and watch them build their own Microsoft Excel to your Lotus 1-2-3, their own Word to your WordPerfect. In your domain. The rational response is to pick sides, split workloads, and keep leverage. A fragmented buyer base does not pay monopoly prices for compute. Winner-take-all pricing requires winner-take-all customers, and the customers are actively organizing against being taken.
10. The 10x ARR growth is history, not a promise. Every step of the bull math compounds off frontier lab revenue growing roughly 10x a year. But listen to how Dario Amodei himself talks about that number. He cites the 10-fold annual growth as what HAS happened, and names the fragility in the same breath: “If I’m just off by a year in that rate of growth, or if the growth rate is 5x a year instead of 10x a year, then you go bankrupt.” Even the ‘crazy’ 80x quarter and the 30 billion dollar run rate are descriptions of the rear-view mirror. Nobody at scale in tech history has sustained 10x annual revenue growth for long, arguably three to five periods at most before the law of large numbers bends every curve. It always has.

...

Prices stay firm through the IPO window and into the 2027 wafer crunch. The bulls are right about the next 18-24 months of tightness, and Dwarkesh has done everyone a service by putting some numbers on it.

But past the window, the spectrum widens rather than the whole curve lifting 10 to 15x. Supply answers the umbrella. Tokens keep deflating. Silicon alternatives compound. Local AI siphons inference off the mainframe. And the buyers refuse to consolidate behind the frontier labs, for reasons that have nothing to do with price and everything to do with survival.

results.title: AI Compute Market 2026: Strategies for Surviving the Shift from Shortage to Oversupply - News and Statistics - IndexBox
highlights:
Major cloud providers have recently reported earnings and raised their capital expenditure plans, partly due to rising costs. On Amazon's July 30 earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy indicated that demand remains strong into 2028, though recouping investment will take several years. He noted that once revenue growth outpaces incremental capital spending, the resulting revenue, free cash flow, and return on invested capital will become compelling.

According to the source, the largest players, such as Nvidia and Google, have secured much of the needed supply capacity due to their massive capital and strong supply chain management. Efficiency is the primary strategy for dealing with supply chain bottlenecks, but other options exist.

Some companies have acquired more resources than they can use. For example, SpaceX merged with xAI, whose models have not generated sufficient demand, and prior to its IPO, SpaceX engaged in multiple AI infrastructure deals using excess capacity. Meta has announced plans to sell or rent excess AI computing power, including a potential $10 billion deal with Anthropic.

...

Everyone with data center AI compute, memory, power, and lasers will profit while supply is short, but eventually supply will catch up with demand, possibly by 2028, 2029, or 2030. The largest and financially strongest companies with strong customer hold are best positioned. These include the fortress companies with P/E ratios of 18 to 36, except AMD with a much higher ratio due to expected GPU share growth. Broadcom and Marvell, leading custom silicon providers, have P/E ratios around 60 as of July 31, but face commoditization risk as hyperscalers increase vendor choice.

...

Neoclouds like Coreweave and Nebius have large valuations despite being unprofitable, having secured compute allocations and contracts. However, when supply exceeds demand, hyperscalers may prioritize their own capacity over renting from neoclouds. Data center AI growth will likely continue despite shortages because big players have secured supply, model optimization reduces demand, and innovative architectures improve performance. Players with windfall profits need to plan for oversupply and develop differentiated, sticky offerings to avoid price crashes.

results.title: The Six-Year-Old Chip That Rents for More Than It Did Last Year
highlights:
The A100 came out in 2020. Two full architectures have shipped since. On CoreWeave’s fourth-quarter call in February, the management said that H100s were recontracting at close to the prices they first carried, and that on A100s “the ASPs are actually trending higher in recent contracts.” To put it plainly: average A100 pricing increased in 2025 (transcript).

That is management talking about its own book, so I looked for someone with no position. GetDeploying tracks 367 A100 listings across 39 providers, and its median on-demand rate has risen about 10 percent since August 2025, from $1.70 to $1.86 an hour (getdeploying). A second aggregator has the A100 roughly flat across the whole stretch from July 2024 to July 2026. Nobody has it falling.

The H100 series is the part that changed my mind, though, because it contains the test I wanted.

H100 rates did collapse. From around $8 an hour in 2023 they fell all the way to about $1.70 by October 2025. If obsolescence were the mechanism, that is where the story ends. Instead the price turned and rose almost 40 percent to $2.35 by March 2026, and on-demand capacity is now reported sold out across essentially every GPU type (SemiAnalysis).

The fall was not the new architecture arriving, it was the shortage ending as Nvidia’s production caught up. When demand caught up in turn, the old parts repriced upward. I had been treating the 2024 to 2025 decline as evidence of decay, and it was evidence of supply normalising.

...

There is a real catch, and it is not the one I was looking for. The rate holds up. The resale value does not. Used A100 80GB boards go for something like $12,000 to $18,000 against $25,000 and up when new, and dealer compilations put the loss on upgrade near half (Hashrate Index). So the machine keeps its worth as a thing that earns rent, and loses a great deal of it as a thing you sell. Anyone whose plan involves selling the hardware is in a different business from anyone who plans to keep renting it.

...

The limit on all of this is that every rate quoted above is a shortage price. Capacity is sold out, which is exactly the condition under which old hardware holds its rate. The difference from a year ago is that we now have one clean observation of what happens when the shortage lifts, and the answer was that rates fell a long way and then came back.

CoreWeave reports its second quarter tomorrow. The line I want is what the older fleet earns per hour against what it earned a year ago. Management has described it twice on calls now, and the next real test is not this print. It is whether those rates hold when the enormous amount of capacity currently under construction actually arrives.

results.title: DigitalOcean launches Spot GPU Droplets for B300, MI355X and MI350X
highlights:
Spot GPU Droplets entered public preview on August 10, 2026. On October 18 the pricing page listed a B300 at $6.17 per GPU-hour; the price is locked when you create the Droplet.

...

DigitalOcean put Spot GPU Droplets into public preview on August 10, 2026. Spot Droplets run on idle GPU capacity at a lower, changing price, and DigitalOcean can take them back when it needs the capacity. They come in single-GPU and 8-GPU sizes. The same day, DigitalOcean opened a data center in Memphis, Tennessee (MEM1), which offers AMD Instinct MI355X Spot GPU Droplets.

## What it costs

DigitalOcean’s pricing page lists three Spot plans. On October 18, 2026, the current prices per GPU per hour were:

| GPU | Spot price (Oct 18) | Spot price (Aug 30) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA HGX B300 | $6.17 | $11.19 |
| AMD Instinct MI355X | $5.50 | $4.50 |
| AMD Instinct MI350X | $3.50 | $4.00 |

The prices move: DigitalOcean’s docs say they may change daily, based on idle GPU capacity, and are never above the on-demand price for the same configuration. The price you see when you create a Droplet is locked for the life of that Droplet.

None of these three GPUs is offered on demand. Without Spot, the B300 is available only on a 12-month reserved plan, at $7.94 per GPU-hour.

## The catch: reclaims

DigitalOcean can reclaim a Spot GPU Droplet to reuse the capacity. The pricing page says it aims to give at least 2 hours’ notice, but in some cases, including emergencies, it may give less notice or none. The notice goes by email to the team account and to the person who created the Droplet. Billing is per second, like on-demand GPU Droplets, and stops when you destroy the Droplet or DigitalOcean reclaims it.

DigitalOcean suggests Spot for batch training, batch or asynchronous inference, hyperparameter tuning and rendering: work that can save its progress and restart elsewhere. For production inference and anything that needs to stay up, it points to on-demand Droplets.

results.title: AI Compute Shortage Shifts Chip Strategy Towards Efficiency | SendTech Times
highlights:
Semiconductor Engineering analysed how AI data-centre growth is being shaped by foundry, memory, power and optical-link bottlenecks as chip buyers look for more tokens from scarce capacity.

...

Semiconductor Engineering analysed AI data-centre growth through the bottlenecks now shaping chip supply, with efficiency presented as the main lever for the next two to five years while foundry capacity, memory, power and optical links remain constrained.

The piece is less a demand forecast than a map of workarounds. Hyperscalers and model developers are trying to extract more tokens from scarce infrastructure through custom silicon, smaller models, routing tools, improved GPUs, optical compute experiments and supply deals for unused capacity.

...

On Amazon’s July 30 earnings call, chief executive Andy Jassy said demand remained strong into 2028, while returns on capital would become clearer once revenue growth outpaced incremental capital expenditure.

The analysis also treated spare capacity as a near-term pressure valve. It cited AI infrastructure agreements linked to xAI and SpaceX, including a $45 billion Anthropic deal for access to 220K Nvidia GPUs and 300MW, plus a $920 million-a-month Google deal through mid-2029 for ~110K GPUs.

...

The supply-chain view keeps the focus on chips rather than general cloud demand. Semiconductor Engineering framed faster accelerators as useful only when packaging, HBM, networking, power delivery and wafer starts arrive in enough volume for production systems. Near-term scarcity can coexist with later buyer pressure for lower-cost, workload-specific hardware once supply improves.

...

The current shortage benefits companies with compute, memory, power and optical-networking capacity. The harder question is what happens if supply catches up with demand around 2028, 2029 or 2030, especially for providers whose valuations assume rented capacity remains scarce.

Differentiation is the unresolved test for chip suppliers, neoclouds and memory vendors. The public gaps are actual optical-compute system performance, future wafer allocation, sustained customer demand for rented GPU capacity, whether specialised HBM becomes a durable product category, binding supply volumes for smaller accelerator startups and customer commitments after the shortage eases.

results.title: SpaceX’s 10GW AI Computing Expansion Plan: From Aerospace Giant to AI Infrastructure Platform—Is Its Stock Growth Logic Being Redefined? | Gate Blog
highlights:
On August 4, 2026, SpaceX dropped a bombshell during its first earnings call since going public. CEO Elon Musk announced that the company plans to add 6 to 8 GW of new computing power in 2027, with potential upside exceeding 10 GW. With capital expenditures estimated at $50 billion per GW, this means SpaceX could spend between $300 billion and $500 billion in 2027—on par with the projected investments of AWS and Google.

...

The AI industry is shifting from "model supremacy" to "compute is power."

...

According to financial disclosures, by the end of Q2 2026, SpaceX had 1.4 GW of available AI compute. This is expected to surpass 2 GW by the end of 2026, with a 2027 year-end target approaching 10 GW. In response to analyst questions, Musk further stated that the provisional goal is to bring 20 GW of power and cooling capacity online by the end of 2027, with a high likelihood of reaching at least 15 GW even if there are delays.

...

Revenue Potential: According to SemiAnalysis’s Tokenomics model and inference simulator, OpenAI and Anthropic’s API inference services on the GB300 cluster can generate over $100 billion in annual revenue per GW. With a conservative rental price of $3 per GPU-hour, annual costs per GW are about $12 billion, yielding inference gross margins above 60%, with flagship models exceeding 85%.

...

Microsoft’s demand for compute is the pivotal variable in SpaceX’s AI compute story. In October 2025, Microsoft signed a $250 billion infrastructure-as-a-service agreement with OpenAI, which SemiAnalysis estimates equates to about 7 GW of compute. This contract has left Microsoft facing severe compute constraints for its Foundry API business and Copilot applications.

...

### Will AI Demand Meet Expectations?

The core question remains whether future compute demand can absorb new capacity. While compute is currently in short supply, if AI commercialization lags or model efficiency significantly reduces per-unit compute consumption, new capacity could face underutilization risks.
